newsitem.title: DUBAI: Caspian oil line faces construction delay - CPC.
newsitem.headline: Caspian oil line faces construction delay - CPC.

text.p: Work on building a $2 billion crude pipeline linking Kazakhstan's Tengiz oilfield to Russia's Black Sea port of Novorossiisk could be delayed by a few months until the middle of 1998, a pipeline official said on Tuesday.

"(Construction start-up) might shift back several months from the original early 1998 date," Ed Smith, general director of the Caspian Pipeline Consortium (CPC), told Reuters on the sidelines of an industry conference in Dubai.

CPC and Russia signed the contract for the construction of the 1,500 km (940 mile) pipeline -- the biggest foreign investment deal in Russian history -- on May 16 pending the completion of feasibility studies, environmental reports and rights of way agreements.

Managers at U.S. oil firm Chevron Corp, the largest single shareholder in the CPC consortium with 15 percent equity, said last month that they expected construction work to begin early next year with pipeline completion set for September 1999.
A revised completion dates for the pipeline was now December 1999, Smith said.
Despite the expected delay in construction, Smith remained upbeat on the project's future.
"We're off and running," Smith said, adding that CPC managers had met Fluor Daniel staff in Houston, Texas last week to discuss technical aspects of the pipeline.

CPC, originally set up in 1992 and now comprising eight companies and three governments, plans to transport about 560,000 barrels per day (bpd) through the pipeline in early stages, building volumes gradually to 1.34 million bpd by 2014.
The line will mainly supply oil from Tengiz and also other Kazakh fields and from deposits in Russian Siberia. Russia will earn as much as $900 million a year from taxes and dividends.
Chevron and Mobil Corp, with their $20 billion Tengiz project, will be CPC's main customers but other producers will be granted access.
Russia's largest oil firm, LUKoil, has a 12.5 percent stake in the CPC consortium and state oil company Rosneft 7.5 percent.
Moscow also owns 24 percent of the consortium and may divide its share equally between LUKoil, Rosneft and the country's oil pipeline monopoly Transneft.
Kazakhstan has 19 percent and Gulf Arab Oman seven percent.

CPC shareholders also include Mobil with 7.5 percent, Britain's BG Plc (formerly British Gas) and Italy's Agip SpA with two percent each and Oryx Energy Co and Munaigaz of Kazakhstan with 1.75 percent each.
U.S. Atlantic Richfield and Royal Dutch Shell Group will also have a stake in the line through partnerships with LUKoil and Rosneft respectively.
Amoco Corp will also use the line.
